newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ police seize "black box" from 1995 air crash.
newsitem.headline: NZ police seize "black box" from 1995 air crash.

text.p: New Zealand police investigating the 1995 crash of an Ansett New Zealand airplane seized the cockpit voice recorder on Friday, ending a lengthy battle over custody of the "black box".

The seizure of the recorder from the headquarters of the Transport Accident Investigation Commission (TAIC) came just hours before accident investigators released a much-delayed report into the crash which included extracts of transcribed material from the black box.

The report concluded that six of the seven causal factors in the accident lay with the crew, while one was technical. Three passengers and a flight attendant died in the crash and 14 people suffered serious injuries.

The pilots' trade union had brought a court case to block police access to the voice records, saying they should not be used to prosecute the two surviving pilots but only to prevent future accidents. It lost the case last month.
The union's action had stalled both the delivery of the accident report and the separate police investigation into possible offences by the surviving pilots.
Both men have been suspended from flying since the Dash 8 aircraft, carrying 18 passengers and three crew, smashed into hilly farmland near Palmerston North, on North Island, on June 9, 1995.
The Transport Accident Investigation Commission's (TAIC) 135-page report showed the flightdeck crew were distracted by an undercarriage problem and failed to notice the aircraft was flying too low.
The edited black box transcript, included in a publicly released report for the first time in New Zealand, indicated laughter in the cockpit just seconds before the plane crashed.

Detective Sergeant Dennis O'Rourke told New Zealand radio that police took the original tapes, transcripts and other materials on Friday morning after executing a search warrant at TAIC headquarters in Wellington.
TAIC accident investigator Ron Chippindale told reporters the recorder had given TAIC a "very clear indication" of the relevance of causal factors in the accident.
The New Zealand Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA) stood by its view that publication of the records was counter-productive.
In a statement, it said it believed the accident report was deficient in several areas.

"(The report) also points to a number of factors not necessarily under the control of any pilot which could reoccur and may reoccur if the lessons to be learned from this accident are not learned and utilised for the future.
"Prosecuting aircrew is not going to achieve that and in all likelihood the lessons would be lost," ALPA added.
Ansett New Zealand, for its part, said the findings of the TAIC report had been useful.
Chief executive Kevin Doddrell told reporters it would be "grossly unfair" of him to comment on any aspect of the accident which might influence the police investigation.
